title: Transmission Line Models
description: Series R and L, shunt C, the short, medium and long line models, ABCD parameters, surge impedance loading and the Ferranti effect.

study.title: Line parameters
study.body: A line has, per unit length: series **resistance** $r$ (rising with temperature, and slightly with frequency through skin effect), series **inductance** $L$ from the magnetic flux around the conductors, shunt **capacitance** $C$ between the conductors and to ground, and a tiny shunt conductance (insulator leakage, corona) that is usually neglected. They are spread along the whole line. On overhead high-voltage lines $\omega L$ is typically 5–15 times $r$, and more on EHV lines with bundled conductors.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}z &= r + j\omega L\\ y &= g + j\omega C \approx j\omega C\end{aligned}

study.title: Geometry: GMD and GMR
study.body: For a transposed three-phase line, $L$ and $C$ per phase depend on the logarithm of the phase spacing, the **geometric mean distance** $D_{eq}$, over the conductor size: its **geometric mean radius** $D_s$ ($0.7788r$ for a solid round conductor, from tables for stranded ones) for $L$, and its outer radius $r$ for $C$. Wider spacing raises $L$ and lowers $C$. A **bundle** of 2–4 subconductors per phase acts like one much fatter conductor: lower $L$, higher $C$ and less corona.

study.title: Short line (up to about 80 km)
study.body: The charging current is negligible, so the line is just its total series impedance $Z = z\ell$. All quantities are per phase: line-to-neutral voltages and line currents.
study.formula: \mathbf V_S = \mathbf V_R + Z\mathbf I_R,\qquad \mathbf I_S = \mathbf I_R

study.title: Medium line: nominal π (about 80–250 km)
study.body: Half of the total shunt admittance $Y = y\ell$ is placed at each end of the series impedance $Z = z\ell$. Writing the result as $\mathbf V_S = A\mathbf V_R + B\mathbf I_R$, $\mathbf I_S = C\mathbf V_R + D\mathbf I_R$:

study.title: Long line: distributed parameters
study.body: Above about 250 km lumping gets inaccurate; the line equations are solved exactly with the **propagation constant** $\gamma = \sqrt{zy} = \alpha + j\beta$ and the **characteristic (surge) impedance** $Z_c = \sqrt{z/y}$. For a **lossless** line ($r = g = 0$): $Z_c = \sqrt{L/C}$ is real (about 250–400 Ω), $\gamma = j\beta$ with $\beta = \omega\sqrt{LC}$, and cosh, sinh become cos and j sin. Waves travel at $1/\sqrt{LC}$, close to the speed of light: β ≈ 0.072°/km at 60 Hz.

study.title: ABCD parameters and regulation
study.body: Every line model (like any linear, reciprocal two-port) can be written in ABCD form, with $AD - BC = 1$. At no load ($\mathbf I_R = 0$) the receiving-end voltage is $V_S/|A|$; since $|A| < 1$ for medium and long lines, it is **higher** than $V_S$ itself (the Ferranti effect). Voltage regulation compares the no-load and full-load receiving-end voltages at fixed $V_S$:

study.title: Surge impedance loading
study.body: A lossless line terminated in its own $Z_c$ carries the **surge impedance load**: the reactive power generated by the shunt capacitance exactly equals that absorbed by the series inductance, so $|V|$ is the same all along the line. Typical SIL: about 50 MW at 138 kV, 400 MW at 345 kV, 900 MW at 500 kV and 2200 MW at 765 kV. Below SIL a line generates net reactive power; above SIL it absorbs it.

study.title: Explore: the Ferranti effect
study.body: Voltage profile of a lossless 60-Hz line with the receiving end held at 1.0 pu and a unity-pf load. At light load the charging current flowing through the series inductance makes the voltage **rise** towards the receiving end, so the sending end needs less than 1.0 pu; equivalently, with $V_S$ fixed the receiving end rises to $V_S/\cos\beta\ell$ at no load. At $P_R$ = SIL the profile is flat; above SIL it sags. Try a long line at no load.

lessons.title: Line parameters and the short line

steps.title: Four distributed parameters
steps.body: Per unit length a line has series resistance $r$ and inductance $L$, and shunt capacitance $C$ and conductance $g$ (usually neglected). $L$ and $C$ come from the geometry: the **geometric mean distance** between the phases, $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{ab}D_{bc}D_{ca}}$, and the conductor's **geometric mean radius** $D_s$ (for $L$) or outer radius $r$ (for $C$).

steps.prompt: A transposed three-phase line has its conductors in a flat row, {{D}} m apart: $D_{ab} = D_{bc}$ = {{D}} m and $D_{ca}$ = {{2*D}} m. Find the geometric mean distance $D_{eq}$ (in m).
steps.explanation: $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{ab}D_{bc}D_{ca}}$ = ∛({{D}} × {{D}} × {{2*D}}) = {{D*2^(1/3)}} m, 26 % more than the adjacent spacing.

steps.prompt: A 60-Hz line has $D_{eq}$ = {{Deq}} m and conductors with a geometric mean radius $D_s$ = {{Ds*1000}} mm.

ask.prompt: Find the inductance per phase of a 1-km length.
ask.explanation: $L = 2\times10^{-7}\ln(D_{eq}/D_s)$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × ln({{Deq}}/{{Ds}}) = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{ln(Deq/Ds)}} = {{L/1000|H}} per metre, or {{L|H}} per km.

ask.prompt: Find the series reactance per phase of the whole {{len}}-km line.

steps.prompt: Each phase conductor of a line is replaced by a bundle of two subconductors with the same total cross-section. What happens to the line parameters?
steps.explanation: The bundle has a much larger equivalent GMR and radius, so $\ln(D_{eq}/D_s)$ and $\ln(D_{eq}/r)$ both shrink: $L$ falls and $C$ rises. Consequently $Z_c = \sqrt{L/C}$ falls and the surge impedance loading rises; the lower surface field also reduces corona.

steps.title: The short-line model
steps.body: Up to about 80 km the charging current is small and the shunt capacitance is neglected: the line is just its total series impedance $Z = (r + j\omega L)\ell$. Per phase, with line-to-neutral voltages:
steps.formula: \mathbf V_S = \mathbf V_R + Z\mathbf I_R,\qquad \mathbf I_S = \mathbf I_R

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, 60-Hz line has $z$ = {{r}} + j{{x}} Ω/km per phase. It delivers {{P|W}} at pf {{pf}} lagging to a load at {{V|V}} (line-to-line). Use the short-line model to find the sending-end line-to-line voltage.
steps.explanation: $Z$ = {{R}} + j{{X}} Ω. $\mathbf V_R$ = {{V/sqrt(3)|V}}∠0°, $I_R$ = {{P|W}}/(1.732 × {{V|V}} × {{pf}}) = {{I|A}} at −{{deg(acos(pf))|°}}. $\mathbf V_S = \mathbf V_R + Z\mathbf I_R$ = {{Vsr|V}} + j{{Vsi|V}}, $|\mathbf V_S|$ = {{sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}}, so $V_{S,LL}$ = {{sqrt(3)*sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: The same kind of line: {{len}} km, $z$ = {{r}} + j{{x}} Ω/km, delivering {{P|W}} at pf {{pf}} lagging and {{V|V}}. The sending-end voltage works out at {{sqrt(3)*Vs|V|5}}. Find the voltage regulation in per cent.
steps.explanation: In the short-line model $A = 1$, so removing the load leaves $V_{R,NL} = V_S$ = {{sqrt(3)*Vs|V|5}}. %VR = ({{sqrt(3)*Vs|V|5}} − {{V|V}})/{{V|V}} × 100 = {{100*(sqrt(3)*Vs - V)/V|%}}.

steps.prompt: In the short-line model, the sending-end and receiving-end currents are equal.
steps.explanation: With the shunt capacitance neglected there is only a series path: $\mathbf I_S = \mathbf I_R$, i.e. $C = 0$ and $D = 1$ in ABCD form. In the medium and long models part of the sending-end current is charging current.

steps.title: The nominal π
steps.body: Between about 80 and 250 km the charging current matters. Place half of the total shunt admittance $Y = j\omega C\ell$ at each end of the series impedance $Z$:

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, {{V|V}} line has $x$ = {{x}} Ω/km and $b$ = {{b*1e6}} µS/km per phase. Neglect resistance and use the nominal π. Find $A$.
steps.explanation: $Z = jX$ with $X$ = {{x}} × {{len}} = {{x*len|Ω}}; $Y = jB$ with $B$ = {{b*1e6}} µS × {{len}} = {{b*len|S}}. $YZ/2 = (jB)(jX)/2 = -XB/2$ = −{{x*len*b*len/2}}, so $A$ = 1 − {{x*len*b*len/2}} = {{1 - x*len*b*len/2||4}}, real and just below 1.

steps.prompt: The {{len}}-km, {{V|V}} line ($x$ = {{x}} Ω/km, $b$ = {{b*1e6}} µS/km, nominal π, resistance neglected) is energized at rated voltage from the sending end, with the receiving end open. Find the receiving-end line-to-line voltage.
steps.explanation: $A = 1 - XB/2$ = 1 − ({{x*len}} Ω × {{b*len|S}})/2 = {{1 - x*len*b*len/2||4}}. With $\mathbf I_R = 0$: $V_R = V_S/A$ = {{V|V}}/{{1 - x*len*b*len/2||4}} = {{V/(1 - x*len*b*len/2)|V|4}}, a rise of {{100*(1/(1 - x*len*b*len/2) - 1)|%}}: the Ferranti effect.

steps.title: The long line
steps.body: Above about 250 km lumping loses accuracy. The exact solution of the line's differential equations uses the propagation constant $\gamma$ and the characteristic impedance $Z_c$:
steps.formula: \begin{aligned}\gamma &= \sqrt{zy},\quad Z_c = \sqrt{z/y}\\ A = D &= \cosh\gamma\ell\\ B &= Z_c\sinh\gamma\ell\\ C &= \sinh(\gamma\ell)/Z_c\end{aligned}

steps.title: The lossless line
steps.body: With $r = g = 0$, $Z_c = \sqrt{L/C}$ is a pure resistance and $\gamma = j\beta$ with $\beta = \omega\sqrt{LC}$. Since $\cosh(j\beta\ell) = \cos\beta\ell$ and $\sinh(j\beta\ell) = j\sin\beta\ell$:

steps.prompt: A lossless line has $L$ = {{L|H}}/km and $C$ = {{C|F}}/km per phase. Find its characteristic impedance $Z_c$.
steps.explanation: $Z_c = \sqrt{L/C}$ = √({{L|H}}/{{C|F}}) = {{sqrt(L/C)|Ω}}. The per-km lengths cancel. Bundled EHV lines have lower $Z_c$ (about 250–300 Ω) than single-conductor lines (350–400 Ω).

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km lossless line has $L$ = {{L|H}}/km and $C$ = {{C|F}}/km and operates at {{f}} Hz. Find its electrical length $\beta\ell$ in degrees.
steps.explanation: $\beta = \omega\sqrt{LC}$ = 2π × {{f}} × √({{L|H}} × {{C|F}}) = {{2*pi*f*sqrt(L*C)||3}} rad/km. $\beta\ell$ = {{2*pi*f*sqrt(L*C)*len||3}} rad = {{deg(2*pi*f*sqrt(L*C)*len)|°}}. The wave speed $1/\sqrt{LC}$ ≈ {{1/sqrt(L*C)||3}} km/s, close to the speed of light.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km lossless 60-Hz line ($\beta$ = 0.00126 rad/km) is energized at {{V|V}} from one end, with the far end open. Find the voltage at the open end.
steps.explanation: $\beta\ell$ = 0.00126 × {{len}} = {{bl}} rad = {{deg(bl)|°}}. At no load $V_R = V_S/A = V_S/\cos\beta\ell$ = {{V|V}}/{{cos(bl)}} = {{V/cos(bl)|V}}, {{100*(1/cos(bl)-1)|%}} above the sending end.

steps.prompt: Match each line model to what it includes.
pairs: Nominal π: Y/2 at each end
steps.explanation: The longer the line, the more charging current and distributed effects matter. The lossless approximation keeps the distributed model but drops r and g, which turns the hyperbolic functions into trigonometric ones.

lessons.title: ABCD, SIL and the Ferranti effect

steps.prompt: A {{V|V}} lossless line with $Z_c$ = {{Zc}} Ω is terminated in its characteristic impedance at rated voltage. Find the line current.
steps.explanation: Per phase the load is $Z_c$, so $I = V_{LN}/Z_c$ = ({{V|V}}/1.732)/{{Zc}} Ω = {{V/(sqrt(3)*Zc)|A}}. The three-phase power is then the SIL, $V^2/Z_c$ = {{V^2/Zc|W}}.

steps.prompt: What is the surge impedance loading of a {{V|V}} line with $Z_c$ = {{Zc}} Ω?
steps.explanation: SIL $= 3V_{LN}^2/Z_c = V_{LL}^2/Z_c$ = ({{V|V}})²/{{Zc}} Ω = {{V^2/Zc|W}}. $3V^2/Z_c$ uses the line-to-line voltage in the per-phase formula; $V^2/(3Z_c)$ is one phase only.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, 60-Hz, {{V|V}} line has $z$ = {{r}} + j{{x}} Ω/km and $y$ = j{{b*1e6}} µS/km per phase. Use the exact long-line model.

ask.explanation: $zy$ has magnitude $b|z|$ = {{b*sqrt(r^2+x^2)||3}} km⁻² and angle {{deg(2*an)|°}}, so $\gamma\ell = \sqrt{zy}\,\ell$ = {{g*len||4}}∠{{deg(an)|°}} = {{al||3}} + j{{be||4}}. $A$ = $\cosh(\alpha\ell + j\beta\ell)$ = $\cosh\alpha\ell\cos\beta\ell + j\sinh\alpha\ell\sin\beta\ell$ = {{Ar||4}} + j{{Ai||3}}, $|A|$ = {{sqrt(Ar^2+Ai^2)||4}}.

ask.prompt: The sending end is held at rated voltage. Find the receiving-end line-to-line voltage at no load.
ask.explanation: $\gamma\ell$ = {{al||3}} + j{{be||4}} (from $\sqrt{zy}\,\ell$), so $A = \cosh\gamma\ell$ = {{Ar||4}} + j{{Ai||3}} and $|A|$ = {{sqrt(Ar^2+Ai^2)||4}}. At no load $V_R = V_S/|A|$ = {{V|V}}/{{sqrt(Ar^2+Ai^2)||4}} = {{V/sqrt(Ar^2+Ai^2)|V|4}}.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km lossless 60-Hz line ($\beta\ell$ = {{deg(bl)|°}}) feeds a unity-pf load whose voltage is held at 1.0 pu. Set the load so that the sending end needs {{Vt}} pu.
steps.explanation: With $\mathbf V_R$ = 1∠0° and $\mathbf I_R = (P_R/\text{SIL})\,\mathbf V_R/Z_c$, the sending end is $\mathbf V_S = \cos\beta\ell + j(P_R/\text{SIL})\sin\beta\ell$. Setting $|\mathbf V_S|$ = {{Vt}}: $P_R/\text{SIL}$ = $\sqrt{({{Vt}}^2 - \cos^2\beta\ell)/\sin^2\beta\ell}$ = {{sqrt((Vt^2 - cos(bl)^2)/sin(bl)^2)}}. Below SIL the voltage rises towards the load; above SIL it falls.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, {{V|V}} line ($x$ = {{x}} Ω/km, $b$ = {{b*1e6}} µS/km, resistance neglected, nominal π) delivers {{P|W}} at pf {{pf}} lagging and rated voltage. Find the sending-end line-to-line voltage.
steps.explanation: $A = 1 - XB/2$ = {{A||4}}, $B = jX$ = j{{x*len|Ω}}. $\mathbf V_R$ = {{V/sqrt(3)|V}}∠0°, $I_R$ = {{I|A}} at −{{deg(acos(pf))|°}}. $\mathbf V_S = A\mathbf V_R + jX\mathbf I_R$ = {{Vsr|V}} + j{{Vsi|V}}, so $|\mathbf V_S|$ = {{sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}} and $V_{S,LL}$ = {{sqrt(3)*sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: A lossless line loaded exactly at its surge impedance loading neither absorbs nor generates net reactive power.
steps.explanation: At SIL, $I = V/Z_c$ everywhere, so per unit length the reactive power absorbed by the inductance, $I^2\omega L$, equals that generated by the capacitance, $V^2\omega C$ (because $V^2/I^2 = L/C$). The voltage profile is flat.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km lossless 60-Hz line ({{V|V}}, $Z_c$ = {{Zc}} Ω, $\beta$ = 0.00126 rad/km) is energized at rated voltage with the far end open. How much reactive power must the source at the sending end **absorb**?
steps.explanation: At no load $\mathbf I_S = C\mathbf V_R$ with $\mathbf V_R = \mathbf V_S/\cos\beta\ell$, so $\mathbf I_S = j\mathbf V_S\tan\beta\ell/Z_c$: it **leads** the voltage, i.e. the line pushes reactive power into the source. Three-phase: $Q = V_{LL}^2\tan\beta\ell/Z_c$ = ({{V|V}})² × tan {{deg(bl)|°}}/{{Zc}} = {{V^2*tan(bl)/Zc|var}}, roughly {{V^2*tan(bl)/Zc/len|var}} per km.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, 500-kV, 60-Hz line has $L$ = {{L|H}}/km and $C$ = {{C|F}}/km per phase; treat it as lossless.

ask.prompt: The sending end is held at 500 kV. Find the receiving-end voltage at no load.

steps.prompt: For a {{len}}-km lossless 60-Hz line with $Z_c$ = {{Zc}} Ω and $\beta$ = 0.00126 rad/km, the exact equivalent π has series reactance $X' = Z_c\sin\beta\ell$. Find $X'$.
steps.explanation: $\beta\ell$ = {{bl}} rad = {{deg(bl)|°}}. $X' = Z_c\sin\beta\ell$ = {{Zc}} × {{sin(bl)}} = {{Zc*sin(bl)|Ω}}. The nominal π would use $\omega L\ell = Z_c\beta\ell$ = {{Zc*bl|Ω}}: {{100*(bl/sin(bl)-1)|%}} too much. The correction factor $\sin\beta\ell/\beta\ell$ matters for long lines.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows $|V|$ along a 500-km lossless line at **no load**, with the sending end held at 1.0 pu?
steps.explanation: At no load $V(x) = V_R\cos\beta x$ with $x$ measured from the open end, so the voltage rises monotonically towards the open end, reaching $V_S/\cos\beta\ell$ = 1/cos 36° ≈ 1.24 pu. A flat profile means loading at SIL; a falling profile means loading above SIL.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km, 500-kV, 60-Hz line has $z$ = 0.03 + j0.33 Ω/km and $y$ = j5.0 µS/km. It delivers {{P|W}} at pf {{pf}} lagging and 500 kV. Using the exact long-line model, find the sending-end line-to-line voltage.
steps.explanation: $Z_c = \sqrt{z/y}$ = {{Zm||4}}∠{{deg(Za)|°}} Ω and $\gamma\ell = \sqrt{zy}\,\ell$ = {{al||3}} + j{{be||4}}. Then $A = \cosh\gamma\ell$ = {{Ar||4}} + j{{Ai||3}} and $B = Z_c\sinh\gamma\ell$ = {{Br||4}} + j{{Bi||4}} Ω. With $\mathbf V_R$ = {{Vr|V}}∠0° and $\mathbf I_R$ = {{Ir|A}} + j({{Ii|A}}): $\mathbf V_S = A\mathbf V_R + B\mathbf I_R$ = {{Vsr|V}} + j{{Vsi|V}}, so $V_{S,LL}$ = √3 × {{sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}} = {{sqrt(3)*sqrt(Vsr^2+Vsi^2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: A {{len}}-km lossless 60-Hz line ({{V|V}}, $Z_c$ = {{Zc}} Ω, $\beta$ = 0.00126 rad/km) has both ends held at rated voltage. Find the steady-state limit: the maximum power it can transfer.
steps.explanation: With the exact π, $X' = Z_c\sin\beta\ell$ = {{Zc*sin(bl)|Ω}}, and $P_{max} = V_SV_R/X'$ = ({{V|V}})²/{{Zc*sin(bl)|Ω}} = {{V^2/(Zc*sin(bl))|W}}. That is SIL/sin βℓ = {{V^2/Zc|W}}/{{sin(bl)}}. The longer the line, the closer this theoretical limit comes to SIL; practical loading, with a stability margin, is lower still.

steps.prompt: At no load, the voltage halfway along a long lossless line is higher than the voltage at its open receiving end.
steps.explanation: With $\mathbf I_R = 0$, $V(x) = V_R\cos\beta x$ where $x$ is the distance from the open end. Since $\cos\beta x < 1$, every point is **lower** than the open end: the voltage rises all the way along the line and peaks at the receiving end.
